metadata.title: Vignette Scripts -- Part 3 of 3 (Vignettes 17-24, Day 3 and aftermath)

vignettes.title: The Cannonade
vignettes.panel_summary: At approximately 1:00pm on July 3, two Confederate signal guns fired in sequence and 170 guns erupted along Seminary Ridge -- the largest artillery bombardment ever seen on the North American continent. The sound was heard in Philadelphia, 140 miles away. Alexander's guns fired for nearly two hours before Pickett stepped off.
vignettes.full_script:
At one o'clock in the afternoon, two signal guns fired from Seminary Ridge.

Then 170 guns fired at once.

The sound was heard in Pittsburgh. Some accounts place it as far as Philadelphia -- 140 miles to the east. The smoke rising from Seminary Ridge was visible for twenty miles. Every gun in Alexander's command, every gun in the Third Corps artillery, every piece that could bear on Cemetery Ridge fired simultaneously and continued firing.

Alexander had positioned his guns with extraordinary care. They stretched for nearly two miles along Seminary Ridge, wheel to wheel in places, the barrels elevated slightly to reach the distant blue line on Cemetery Ridge. The Washington Artillery of New Orleans -- the most famous artillery unit in the Confederate army -- was in the line. Pegram's battalion fired from the northern end. Cabell's and Henry's battalions fired from the south.

On Cemetery Ridge, the Union infantry pressed themselves flat behind the stone walls and into the shallow hollows and swales of the ground. The Confederate fire was intense but, as Hunt had feared, much of it was overshooting -- landing behind the ridge near the Taneytown Road, destroying caissons and limbers, killing horses and headquarters staff, nearly hitting Meade himself.

Hunt watched the fire carefully. He began deliberately silencing the Union guns -- battery by battery, pulling them back or having them cease fire. He was conserving ammunition for what he knew was coming. Hancock, riding the line and watching his infantry press closer to the ground, overruled him on some batteries: keep firing, he said. The men need to see their guns fighting.

For nearly two hours the ground shook.

Then Alexander sent his first message to Pickett.

And then the guns fell silent, and across the open fields of Pennsylvania, 12,500 men in gray and butternut stepped out of the tree line and began to walk east.

vignettes.title: Cushing's Battery
vignettes.panel_summary: Lieutenant Alonzo Cushing served his last two guns at The Angle through the Confederate cannonade and Pickett's assault, twice wounded but refusing to leave. He was killed while firing at Armistead's men crossing the wall -- shot through the mouth. He received the Medal of Honor in 2014, 151 years after his death -- the longest gap between action and award in the history of the decoration.
vignettes.full_script:
Alonzo Cushing was twenty-two years old.

He had graduated from West Point in 1861 and commanded Battery A, 4th US Artillery -- six three-inch rifles positioned directly behind the stone wall at The Angle, at the exact focal point of the Confederate assault.

The cannonade had been brutal for his battery. Horses killed. Men down. Two of his six guns disabled. By the time Pickett's infantry appeared at the tree line, Cushing had four guns serviceable and was wounded himself -- a fragment through the shoulder.

As the Confederate line crossed the Emmitsburg Road and came on, Cushing took another hit. The wound was grave -- a shell fragment through the groin. His sergeant, Frederick Fuger, urged him to go to the rear.

Cushing refused. He had two guns left. He would serve them himself.

With Fuger's help, he moved his last two guns to the wall itself -- the stone wall at The Angle -- and loaded them with double canister. As Armistead's men climbed over the wall on his left, as the Union line bent and buckled around him, Cushing fired one last round of canister into the Confederate infantry at a range of perhaps twenty yards.

He was shot through the mouth.

Fuger assumed command of what remained of the battery. The Angle held.

Cushing's family petitioned for a Medal of Honor for the next century and a half. The Army reviewed the case repeatedly. Bureaucratic obstacles -- the statute of limitations, administrative requirements -- delayed the award for generations.

On November 6, 2014, President Obama presented the Medal of Honor to a descendant of Cushing's family at a White House ceremony. Alonzo Cushing received the nation's highest military honor 151 years after he died earning it -- the longest gap between action and award in the history of the decoration.

He was twenty-two years old.

vignettes.title: Pickett's Return
vignettes.panel_summary: After the repulse of Pickett's Charge, Lee rode forward to meet his broken men and told them repeatedly: 'It is all my fault.' General Pickett, asked by Lee to reform his division for defense, replied: 'General Lee, I have no division.' Pickett never forgave Lee for ordering the charge and never recovered from the loss of his men.
vignettes.full_script:
George Pickett sat on his horse and watched his division come back.

They came in clusters and straggles, the survivors of a mile-wide charge across open ground under artillery and musketry. Some walked steadily. Some stumbled. Some were helping others walk. All of them had the look of men who had been through something that no words could explain.

Of the three brigades Pickett had sent forward -- Garnett, Kemper, Armistead -- Garnett was dead, Kemper was critically wounded and briefly a prisoner, Armistead was dying beyond the stone wall he had crossed. The division had suffered nearly 2,700 casualties from 5,500 engaged. Forty-nine percent.

Lee rode forward to meet them.

He rode along the broken line, and he said to them, over and over, the same thing: 'It is all my fault. It is I who have lost this fight, and you must help me out of it the best you can.'

Pickett came to Lee. Lee told him to reform his division -- there might be a Union counterattack coming.

Pickett looked at Lee. 'General Lee,' he said, 'I have no division.'

Lee never acknowledged, officially or privately, that ordering the charge had been a mistake. He praised the courage of his men and said that more support should have been provided. In his official report he blamed himself in the most general terms.

Pickett blamed Lee specifically. For the rest of his life he told anyone who would listen that Lee had destroyed his division. When someone praised Lee in Pickett's presence years after the war, Pickett said quietly: 'That man destroyed my division.'

He said it with the measured tone of a man who had been carrying the weight of it for decades.

vignettes.title: Custer at East Cavalry Field
vignettes.panel_summary: Three miles east of Gettysburg, while Pickett's infantry was being repulsed at The Angle, Stuart's cavalry attempted to sweep around the Union rear. The 23-year-old General George Armstrong Custer personally led the Michigan Brigade in a mounted charge that stopped Stuart cold. 'Come on, you Wolverines!' he shouted -- and they came.
vignettes.full_script:
George Armstrong Custer was twenty-three years old and had been a brigadier general for exactly eight days.

He had earned the promotion through a combination of extraordinary courage and extraordinary luck -- the kind of officer who seemed to attract bullets that always missed. He wore a custom uniform of black velvet with gold trim that made him conspicuous on any battlefield. He wore his hair in long golden ringlets. He was, in the Army of the Potomac, impossible to ignore.

On the afternoon of July 3, while Pickett's infantry was crossing the open fields toward Cemetery Ridge, Stuart's cavalry moved east of Gettysburg to sweep around the Union rear. If Stuart could strike the Union rear simultaneously with the infantry assault on the front, the Army of the Potomac might be destroyed.

Gregg's cavalry division blocked the road. Custer's Michigan Brigade -- 1,900 troopers on fresh horses -- was the striking force.

Stuart advanced. Hampton's South Carolinians and Fitz Lee's Virginians moved forward in what Confederate veterans later described as a magnificent charge -- thousands of horsemen covering the ground in a sweeping wall of cavalry.

Custer rode to the front of his brigade. He turned to his Wolverines.

'Come on, you Wolverines!'

He spurred his horse directly at the Confederate advance. The Michigan Brigade came with him.

The two lines met at a full gallop in the largest cavalry engagement of the Gettysburg campaign. Men sabre'd each other at close range, horses went down, the lines interpenetrated and dissolved into a melee of individual combats across a half-mile front. Hampton was wounded -- a sabre cut to the head.

When it was over, Stuart's cavalry fell back. The Union rear was secure.

On Cemetery Ridge, the last of Pickett's men were streaming back from The Angle.

Custer had done his part.

vignettes.title: Farnsworth's Charge
vignettes.panel_summary: General Elon Farnsworth had been a general for eight days when Kilpatrick ordered him to charge Confederate infantry over rocky terrain south of the battlefield. Farnsworth protested that the charge was suicidal. Kilpatrick insisted. Farnsworth led the charge and was killed. He had been a general for exactly four days when he died.
vignettes.full_script:
Elon Farnsworth had been a general for eight days.

He had the promotion because he was a good cavalry officer and because his uncle was an influential congressman and because Pleasonton was promoting young men he trusted. Eight days -- long enough to receive the commission, pin on the stars, and die.

Kilpatrick ordered him to charge.

Farnsworth looked at the ground ahead. It was a nightmare of boulders and fencing and rocky terrain, defended by Law's Confederate infantry and the dismounted men of Robertson's Texas Brigade. Cavalry -- even the best cavalry -- could not charge formed infantry over ground like that.

He said so.

Kilpatrick, in the accounts that survive, challenged his courage. The exact words are disputed, but the meaning was clear: charge, or be thought a coward.

Farnsworth's face went white. Then he said something that the men nearby remembered for the rest of their lives -- an expression of outrage, of contempt, and of acceptance, all in one breath. He would lead the charge himself.

'If you order the charge, I will lead it,' he said. 'But if we go in there it will be a charge of death.'

Kilpatrick ordered the charge.

Farnsworth rode to the front of his brigade and led them forward into the rocks and the Confederate fire.

He was shot five times. He fell among the boulders south of Big Round Top, a general for four days.

The charge accomplished nothing. No Confederate position was taken, no Union position was relieved. The men who survived came back to their starting line having given nothing and gained nothing.

Kilpatrick's decision was condemned then and has been condemned since. He spent the rest of his life defending it.

vignettes.title: Mudge and the Charge at Culp's Hill
vignettes.panel_summary: Lieutenant Colonel Charles Mudge was ordered to lead his 2nd Massachusetts Infantry in a charge across open ground toward Confederate positions at Culp's Hill. He protested the order. When told it was confirmed, he said: 'It is murder but it is the order.' He led the charge and was killed instantly. The regiment suffered 43% casualties in minutes.
vignettes.full_script:
The order came down at approximately 7:30 in the morning of July 3.

Colonize Silas Colgrove had received instructions to clear Confederate infantry from their position at the base of Culp's Hill. The 2nd Massachusetts and the 27th Indiana were to charge across an open meadow -- perhaps 200 yards of ground fully exposed to Confederate fire from the woods beyond.

Lieutenant Colonel Charles Mudge commanded the 2nd Massachusetts. He read the order and then read it again.

He sent an aide back to Colgrove. Was the order correct? Had there been a mistake?

The aide came back. The order was confirmed.

Mudge looked at the meadow. He looked at his regiment -- 316 men who had served through two years of war, who had marched from Maryland to Pennsylvania, who trusted him.

He turned to his officers.

'It is murder,' he said. 'But it is the order.'

He drew his saber and led the 2nd Massachusetts across the meadow at the double-quick.

The Confederate fire from the woods was immediate and accurate. Men fell as they ran. Mudge was hit almost at once -- shot through the throat, killed instantly, falling in the open ground he had called murder to cross.

The regiment reached the Confederate position, could not hold it, and withdrew. In the few minutes of the charge and its aftermath, 136 of 316 men were casualties -- 43 percent.

The 27th Indiana charged alongside them. It did not go better.

Colgrove's charge is still debated. Some accounts suggest the order was given in confusion, that it was never meant to be a frontal assault across open ground. Whatever the intent, the result was exactly what Mudge had predicted.

His last words -- 'It is murder but it is the order' -- are among the most quoted of the battle.

vignettes.title: Lee Meets His Men
vignettes.trigger_location: Open fields west of Cemetery Ridge
vignettes.panel_summary: As the survivors of Pickett's Charge streamed back toward Seminary Ridge, Robert E. Lee rode out to meet them personally, telling them repeatedly: 'It is all my fault.' Imboden, who was with Lee that evening, described him pacing back and forth saying 'Too bad. Too bad. Oh, too bad.' It was the closest Lee ever came to public acknowledgment of error.
vignettes.full_script:
General John Imboden had been ordered to prepare for the retreat. He was waiting near Lee's headquarters when the survivors of Pickett's Charge began coming back across the fields.

Lee rode out to meet them.

He rode slowly along the broken line of men, and Imboden watched from nearby. What he saw, he wrote later, he never forgot.

Lee rode among his men and said to them, over and over: 'All this has been my fault -- it is I who have lost this fight, and you must help me out of it the best you can.' Some of the men reached up and touched his boots as he passed. Some wept.

When Pickett came to him, Lee said: 'Come, General Pickett. This has been my fight, and upon my shoulders rests the blame.'

That night, Lee found Imboden waiting for him.

'General,' Imboden said, 'this has been a hard day on you.'

Lee said nothing at first. He sat on his horse in the darkness. Then he began to talk, and Imboden wrote down what he said as carefully as he could remember:

'I never saw troops behave more magnificently than Pickett's division of Virginians did today in that grand charge upon the enemy. And if they had been supported as they were to have been -- but for some reason not yet fully explained -- the charge would have been gloriously successful.'

Then Lee fell silent again. He seemed to be speaking almost to himself.

'Too bad. Too bad. Oh, too bad.'

Imboden heard him say it over and over as they rode back toward headquarters.

Lee never said it quite so plainly again.

vignettes.title: The High Water Mark
vignettes.panel_summary: The Battle of Gettysburg ended on July 3, 1863 with approximately 51,000 casualties across three days -- the bloodiest battle ever fought on American soil. The spot where Armistead fell at The Angle is marked today as the High Water Mark of the Confederacy. The Army of Northern Virginia would never again invade the North.
vignettes.full_script:
The battle was over.

From the first shot on Knoxlyn Ridge on the morning of July 1 to the last cavalry action east of town on the afternoon of July 3, the Battle of Gettysburg had consumed three days and approximately 51,000 men. Seven thousand were dead. The rest were wounded or missing. The fields and orchards and woodlots of Adams County, Pennsylvania -- farmland, ordinary farmland -- were covered with the wreckage of two armies.

On July 4, while the town of Gettysburg tried to count its dead, the news arrived from the west: Vicksburg had fallen. Grant had split the Confederacy. Two disasters in two days.

Lee began his retreat on July 4 in a driving rainstorm. Imboden's wagon train -- seventeen miles of it, filled with wounded men who screamed with every jolt of the road -- moved south and west toward Virginia. The army followed, battered, depleted, but intact. Meade chose not to pursue aggressively. The opportunity to destroy Lee's army, if it existed, was not taken.

The Confederacy would fight on for nearly two more years. There would be Cold Harbor and the Wilderness and Petersburg and the Shenandoah and Appomattox. But the moment when Confederate victory was possible -- the moment when a successful invasion of the North might have forced a negotiated peace -- had passed on the afternoon of July 3 at a stone wall in Pennsylvania.

The copse of trees still stands. The stone wall has been rebuilt where it was torn apart in the fighting. A bronze marker -- placed by veterans, not the government -- stands near the spot where Armistead fell.

It reads: 'The High Water Mark of the Rebellion.'

The ground is quiet now. The fields are green in summer, brown in fall, white in winter. The monuments stand in long rows along Seminary Ridge and Cemetery Ridge and the slopes of Culp's Hill and Little Round Top. There are 1,328 of them -- more monuments per square mile than anywhere else on earth.

In July, when the heat is heavy and the air still, you can stand at The Angle and look west across the open fields and understand exactly what happened here, and why it mattered, and what it cost.
